title: Anatomy of a modern scam economy
body_md:
## Follow the money, not the polish
A scam can involve several people or services, but you rarely need to identify them to protect yourself. Follow four functions: **reach** (an ad or message finds you), **credibility** (a plausible employer, friend or brand), **extraction** (money, credentials, access or a payment change) and **cash-out** (moving value beyond easy recall). One person may do every part; in another operation, roles are split. Do not infer a large criminal organization from a polished message. In one documented 2025 FBI case, a provider supplied hosting and domain infrastructure used by many fraudulent investment sites. Other operations may reuse fake pages, contact lists or payment intermediaries; the exact arrangement is not visible from a single message.

A job ad may be the recruitment surface. A chat operator builds trust. A fake dashboard shows a balance. The instruction to deposit funds or relay a payment is the extraction point. If you are asked to receive and send money through your own account, you may be recruited as a *money mule*, even if the arrangement is described as payroll or a customer refund. An incoming transfer does not establish that it is final, lawful or yours to forward. The FTC warns that a deposited check can later prove fake, leaving the recipient liable for money already sent on.

### Where a pause helps
The useful question is not “Which criminal role wrote this?” It is “What asset am I about to hand over, and can I verify the reason through a channel I chose?” Before giving account details, paying to unlock a task, forwarding money, or changing a supplier account, stop the workflow. Contact the genuine organization using an established site, app or number. For a workplace payment, follow a documented approval path and verify changed details with the known supplier contact; a familiar mailbox can itself be compromised.

### What the model cannot tell you
A real company can use recruiters, chat support, dashboards and subcontractors. A slow reply or unusual wording does not prove fraud; a professional website does not prove legitimacy. The strongest decision points are requests that transfer control: advance payment to earn wages, use of your personal account to move another party's funds, credentials, remote access, or an unexpected recipient change. Treat this chain as a way to identify the next safe action, not as a diagnosis of every person in it.

**Remember:** you can interrupt a chain before its last step. If you already moved money, stop further transfers and promptly contact your bank or payment provider. Recovery is uncertain and rules vary by country.

widget_config.goal: Map an apparent opportunity into recruitment, trust-building, extraction and cash-out, then choose where to stop it.
widget_config.today_action: Write down one rule for offers involving your own account: never receive and forward money for a stranger or supposed employer.
widget_config.scope: Global educational model. The FTC examples and reporting routes cited below concern the US; roles vary between schemes and one clue cannot prove a crime.

blocks.title: A paid “quality tester” queue
blocks.situation: Synthetic: A recruiter contacts Mira about rating product photos. A dashboard shows commissions, then says she must deposit a small amount to unlock a higher-paying batch.
blocks.analysis: The first two stages recruit and create a believable balance. The deposit is extraction; a displayed balance is not proof of withdrawable earnings. Mira should stop, use the employer’s independently found careers page, and avoid any deposit.

blocks.title: A real supplier changes a billing contact
blocks.situation: Synthetic: A known print supplier sends a new invoice after a documented change of accountant. The request appears in the usual work system, with no demand to bypass approvals.
blocks.analysis: This can be legitimate. The changed recipient still deserves a call to the supplier number already on file and the normal dual approval. Verification can confirm the change without accusing the supplier.

blocks.title: Trace a synthetic task-job chain
blocks.setup: You are offered a remote catalogue-review role. No real account, link or money is involved in this exercise. At each step, identify the asset at risk.

steps.prompt: A chat recruiter offers immediate work under a famous retailer name. What starts the check?

choices.text: Send your identity document in chat to reserve the role.
choices.consequence: The stranger receives sensitive data before the employer is verified.
choices.explanation: Brand names in a chat are easy to claim.

choices.text: Find the role through the retailer’s own careers page.
choices.consequence: You can compare the role and recruiter without sharing details.
choices.explanation: An independently reached source tests the recruitment claim.

steps.prompt: A dashboard shows a small “earned” balance, but withdrawal requires a deposit. Choose.

choices.text: Decline the deposit and preserve the message privately.
choices.consequence: You avoid paying to access a displayed number.
choices.explanation: A platform display does not make the balance real.

choices.text: Pay once because the balance is larger.
choices.consequence: You risk losing the deposit and being pressured for more.
choices.explanation: A larger displayed number is controlled by the same unknown operator.

steps.prompt: The recruiter says a customer refund will enter your bank and you must forward it. Choose.

choices.text: Forward it after it appears in your account.
choices.consequence: The payment can later be reversed or disputed.
choices.explanation: Seeing a credit is not proof that the money is safe to pass on.

choices.text: Refuse to receive or relay the funds.
choices.consequence: Your account is not used as a transfer channel.
choices.explanation: The FTC warns this can be a money-mule pattern.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: another applicant says they already forwarded a supposed customer refund. What should you advise now?

choices.text: Tell them to stop further transfers, contact their bank promptly through a known channel, and keep the records.
choices.consequence: They can report the transfer and ask about account-specific safeguards; recovery is not guaranteed.
choices.explanation: Once money has moved, prompt provider contact matters as well as stopping the chain.

choices.text: Tell them to wait for the recruiter to reassure them.
choices.consequence: Further transfers may be requested while the completed transfer goes unreported.
choices.explanation: The person who requested the transfer cannot independently assess or resolve it.

blocks.debrief: On replay, identify what you handed over. Sending an identity document in the opening chat gives a stranger a copy of sensitive data: that is already a transfer of control. If you did not send it, the deposit is the next possible handover of value. The refund request adds a risk of moving someone else's funds through your account. If you sent the document, stop sharing data, consult official guidance in your country on exposed identity documents, and watch for misuse. If you paid a deposit or forwarded funds, stop further transfers and promptly contact your bank or payment provider through a known channel; recovery is uncertain. The separate final snapshot concerns another applicant who already forwarded funds, so advise them on that money-transfer response. A genuine job can be verified without using your account as a relay.

blocks.title: Apply the chain to a new offer

questions.prompt: A seller asks to replace the bank account on an existing invoice. Which stage is at risk?

choices.text: Only recruitment; the invoice already exists.
choices.explanation: A real invoice can be used to redirect a payment.

choices.text: No risk if the email signature is correct.
choices.explanation: Signatures can be copied and mailboxes compromised.

choices.text: Payment extraction or diversion; verify the change with the known supplier contact.
choices.explanation: The asset is the outgoing payment, even when the invoice is familiar.

questions.prompt: Why is a small successful withdrawal from an unfamiliar investment portal weak proof?

choices.text: Any withdrawal proves the regulator licensed it.
choices.explanation: A transaction does not establish licensing.

choices.text: The operator may control the display and early withdrawals to build trust.
choices.explanation: A small payout does not establish the safety of later deposits.

questions.prompt: A real employer uses a chat interview. What is the sound conclusion?

choices.text: Chat alone is inconclusive; verify the role and avoid advance payments.
choices.explanation: The channel is common, while a deposit-to-work request changes the risk.

choices.text: Every chat interview is a scam.
choices.explanation: Legitimate employers may use chat tools.

questions.prompt: You already forwarded an unknown “refund.” What is the next step?

choices.text: Forward another payment to settle the account.
choices.explanation: More transfers can increase loss and exposure.

choices.text: Stop further transfers and contact your bank promptly.
choices.explanation: The bank can advise on a potentially reversible or disputed transfer.
